punjab.name: Punjab
punjab.tagline: Fertile plains, winter fields and a food culture shaped by farming and hospitality.

dishes.name: Sarson da Saag with Makki di Roti
dishes.descriptor: Winter greens with maize flatbread
dishes.overview: A winter meal of slow-cooked mustard greens with hand-patted maize flatbread. It is often finished with ghee or white butter and served with radish, jaggery or lassi.
steps: Wash and chop the greens. Simmer with ginger, garlic, chillies, salt and a little water until soft.
Mash or blend coarsely. Add a little maize-flour slurry if a thicker saag is preferred.
Temper with ghee, garlic and optional onion; simmer until combined.
Mix maize flour with warm water and salt. Pat into flat rounds by hand.
Cook on a hot griddle, turning carefully. Finish with ghee or butter and serve with the saag.
dishes.history: The pairing grew from the rhythm of Punjabi winter farming. Mustard greens were gathered in season, while maize became an important grain across the northwestern plains. Rural households brought the two together in a filling winter meal, and the combination later became a familiar emblem of Punjabi food in village homes, roadside dhabas and city restaurants.

dishes.name: Chole Bhature
dishes.descriptor: Spiced chickpeas with puffed fried bread
dishes.overview: Spiced chickpeas simmered in a thick masala and served with deep-fried, leavened bhature. Pickled onion, chutney and green chilli often accompany it.
ingredients: Coriander, cumin, chilli and garam masala
Maida or wheat flour, yoghurt and leavening
steps: Soak chickpeas overnight and cook until tender.
Cook onion, ginger and garlic. Add tomato and spices to make a thick masala.
Add chickpeas and some cooking liquid; simmer until the gravy thickens.
Make a soft dough with flour, yoghurt, salt and leavening. Rest, then roll into rounds.
Deep-fry until puffed and golden. Serve hot with the chole.
dishes.history: The pairing took shape in the bustling food culture of North Indian towns, where hearty chickpea curries were served alongside breads from Punjabi kitchens. After Partition, Punjabi cooks and food businesses carried the combination into Delhi and other cities. Street stalls and neighbourhood restaurants helped turn it into a much-loved breakfast and everyday meal.

regionalGeography.text: Punjab’s fertile alluvial plains, rivers and extensive canal irrigation support wheat, rice, mustard and dairy farming. Hot summers and cool winters shape the growing seasons, while the wetter foothills contrast with the drier south-west.

foodCulture.text: Wheat rotis, rice, dal, seasonal vegetables, curd and buttermilk are common everyday foods. Sarson da saag, makki di roti, stuffed parathas and tandoor breads are popular, with local habits varying across the region.

west-bengal.name: West Bengal
west-bengal.tagline: A river-and-delta cuisine shaped by rice, fish, mustard and sweets.

dishes.name: Shorshe Ilish
dishes.descriptor: Hilsa cooked with mustard and green chilli
dishes.overview: Hilsa is cooked in a pungent mustard paste with green chillies, turmeric and mustard oil. It may be steamed or gently simmered; the sharp sauce balances the fish's rich flavour.
steps: Soak mustard seeds briefly, then grind with green chillies, salt and a little water.
Rub the fish with turmeric and salt.
Warm mustard oil. Add the mustard paste with water and green chillies.
Add the fish and steam or simmer gently until just cooked. Avoid stirring roughly.
dishes.history: Hilsa has long followed the rivers and estuaries of Bengal, making it part of the region's seasonal fishing and food culture. Mustard, grown and pressed across eastern India, became a defining partner for the rich fish. The dish moved between home kitchens and festive meals, and hilsa itself became closely associated with the monsoon and Bengali food identity.

dishes.name: Banglar Rosogolla
dishes.descriptor: Chhana dumplings poached in sugar syrup
dishes.overview: Fresh chhana is kneaded into smooth balls, cooked in boiling sugar syrup and left to soak. The texture depends on the chhana, kneading and syrup.
ingredients: A little semolina or flour in some versions
steps: Curdle hot milk with lemon juice or another food acid; drain the chhana in a clean cloth.
Rinse and press until moist but not watery.
Knead until smooth and roll into crack-free balls.
Boil sugar and water. Add the balls with enough room to expand.
Cook until spongy, then cool in the syrup before serving.
dishes.history: Bengal's sweet shops helped shape the modern rosogolla into a celebrated urban confection. In nineteenth-century Calcutta, confectioners developed new ways of working with chhana, and Nabin Chandra Das became closely associated with the light, syrup-soaked version. Later, family businesses such as K. C. Das helped carry rosogolla beyond local shops through packaged sweets and wider distribution.

regionalGeography.text: West Bengal stretches from Himalayan foothills across fertile river plains to the Ganga delta and coast. Monsoon rain supports rice fields, while rivers, ponds, wetlands and estuaries provide freshwater and brackish-water fish.

foodCulture.text: Rice is usually served with dal, vegetables and fish or meat. Mustard-flavoured fish, posto, street snacks and milk-based sweets are familiar foods; everyday meals and ingredients differ between the hills, western districts and delta.

tamil-nadu.name: Tamil Nadu
tamil-nadu.tagline: A varied food culture shaped by paddy fields, dry plains, coastal trade and temple towns.

dishes.name: Sakkarai Pongal
dishes.descriptor: Sweet rice and lentils for the harvest festival
dishes.overview: Rice and moong dal are cooked until soft, then sweetened with jaggery and finished with ghee, cardamom, cashews and raisins. It is closely associated with Thai Pongal.
steps: Rinse the rice and roast the moong dal lightly.
Cook both with water or milk until very soft.
Dissolve jaggery in a little water and strain.
Stir the syrup into the rice mixture and simmer briefly.
Finish with ghee, cardamom, cashews and raisins.
dishes.history: Sweet pongal belongs to the harvest celebrations of Tamil households. At Thai Pongal, newly harvested rice is cooked as an offering of gratitude for the land, the Sun and the animals that support farming. Over generations, jaggery, ghee and fragrant additions made the preparation a central festive food, shared at home and offered in temples.

dishes.name: Chicken Chettinad
dishes.descriptor: Chicken in a freshly ground, aromatic spice masala
dishes.overview: Chicken is simmered in a freshly ground masala that often includes pepper, fennel, dried chillies, coconut and local spices. Recipes differ between Chettinad households.
ingredients: Dried red chillies, cinnamon and cloves
Kalpasi or other local spices, where used
steps: Dry-roast the whole spices and coconut; cool and grind.
Sauté curry leaves, onion, ginger and garlic in oil.
Add tomato and the ground masala. Cook until aromatic.
Add chicken, salt and a little water. Cover and cook until tender.
Reduce the gravy to the preferred consistency and finish with curry leaves.
dishes.history: Chettinad cooking was shaped by the journeys and trading networks of the Nattukottai Chettiar community. Connections across South and Southeast Asia brought ingredients and culinary ideas into local kitchens, where cooks developed distinctive roasted spice blends. Chicken Chettinad grew from this layered household tradition and later reached a much wider audience through Chettinad restaurants.

foodCulture.text: Rice meals with sambar, rasam and vegetables are common. Idli, dosa, millet dishes, seafood and meat preparations are also popular; Chettinad, Kongunadu, delta and coastal traditions use different ingredients and spice blends.

kerala.name: Kerala
kerala.tagline: A coastal and backwater cuisine built around rice, coconut, spices and shared meals.

dishes.name: Kerala Sadya
dishes.descriptor: A ceremonial vegetarian feast served on a banana leaf
dishes.overview: Sadya is a ceremonial vegetarian feast served on a banana leaf. Rice is accompanied by curries, vegetable dishes, pickles, savouries and payasam; the exact menu varies.
ingredients: Curry leaves, mustard seeds and chillies
steps: Prepare the dishes separately: dal, sambar, avial, thoran, olan, pachadi and pickles are common examples.
Cook the rice and place a clean banana leaf before the guest.
Arrange the accompaniments in the customary order; local practice varies.
Serve rice with the curries and side dishes.
Finish with payasam and the customary savouries.
dishes.history: Large communal meals have long been part of Kerala's temple, harvest and household celebrations. The sadya grew within this culture of hospitality, where a shared meal marked an important occasion and brought seasonal produce from the surrounding region to the table. Onam made one form especially recognisable, while temple festivals, weddings and family gatherings kept the wider feast tradition alive.

dishes.name: Puttu and Kadala Curry
dishes.descriptor: Steamed rice cylinders with black-chickpea curry
dishes.overview: Puttu is steamed rice flour layered with grated coconut. It is commonly served with kadala curry, a spiced black-chickpea preparation.
ingredients: Onion or shallots, ginger and garlic
Coconut oil, mustard seeds and curry leaves
steps: Soak black chickpeas overnight and cook until tender.
Roast coconut, shallots, chilli and coriander; grind to a paste.
Temper mustard seeds and curry leaves. Add onion, chickpeas and the paste; simmer.
Moisten rice flour with salted water until crumbly, not dough-like.
Layer rice flour and coconut in a puttu steamer; steam until cooked.
dishes.history: Puttu became a familiar part of Kerala's everyday food culture in rice-growing communities where coconut was also a common household ingredient. Steaming offered a practical way to turn rice flour into a satisfying meal, while pulses made a substantial accompaniment. The pairing of puttu with kadala curry became a classic breakfast across Kerala, especially in Malabar and coastal towns.

regionalGeography.text: Kerala’s coast, backwaters and Western Ghats bring heavy monsoon rain and varied growing conditions. Lowlands support rice and coconut, while the hills grow spices such as pepper and cardamom; rivers and coastal waters support fishing.

foodCulture.text: Rice, fish curries and coconut-based dishes are common, alongside puttu, appam, idiyappam and tapioca. Sadya is served for festivals, while Malabar, central Kerala and Travancore have distinct dishes and community food traditions.

rajasthan.name: Rajasthan
rajasthan.tagline: A cuisine shaped by arid landscapes, durable ingredients and hospitality.

dishes.name: Dal Baati Churma
dishes.descriptor: Baked wheat rolls, lentils and sweetened crushed bread
dishes.overview: Baati (firm wheat rolls) is served with lentil dal and churma, a sweet made from crushed wheat and ghee. It is a well-known Rajasthani meal served at family gatherings and feasts.
steps: Make a firm wheat dough with ghee, salt and water; shape into balls.
Bake or roast the baati until browned and cooked through.
Cook the lentils until soft; temper with ghee and spices.
Crush some baati and mix with jaggery or sugar and ghee for churma.
Serve baati with dal, churma and chutney.
dishes.history: Dal baati grew from the food traditions of Rajasthan's dry regions, where wheat, pulses and ghee were important parts of the household store. Baati was well suited to cooking over local hearths and carrying on journeys; dal made the meal complete, while churma added a festive sweet element. The combination moved from practical household food into feasts and celebrations.

dishes.overview: Seasoned gram-flour dough is shaped into logs, boiled and sliced. The pieces are simmered in a tangy yoghurt gravy.
steps: Mix besan with salt, spices, carom seeds and a little oil; add water to form a firm dough.
Roll into logs and simmer in salted water until cooked.
Cool and slice the logs into discs.
Whisk yoghurt with spices and a little water.
Temper cumin and asafoetida, add the yoghurt mixture and gatte, then simmer gently.
dishes.history: In Rajasthan's dry climate, cooks made inventive use of ingredients that could be stored in the household pantry. Gram flour became a dependable base for substantial meals, while yoghurt and spices brought richness to everyday cooking. Gatte ki sabzi grew from this style of resourceful regional cooking and became a familiar part of meals across Rajasthan.

regionalGeography.text: Rajasthan’s Thar Desert, Aravalli range and semi-arid plains bring low and uneven rainfall. Sandy soils and water scarcity favour hardy crops such as bajra, pulses and gram, while wetter eastern areas support a wider range of crops.

foodCulture.text: Bajra and wheat breads, pulses, dairy, gram-flour dishes and preserved vegetables are common. Dal baati churma, gatte ki sabzi and ker-sangri are familiar foods, with preferences varying between Marwar, Mewar and eastern districts.

gujarat.name: Gujarat
gujarat.tagline: A cuisine of seasonal vegetables, grains, pulses and fermented foods.

dishes.name: Undhiyu
dishes.descriptor: Winter vegetables slow-cooked in an inverted clay pot
dishes.overview: Undhiyu combines winter vegetables, beans, stuffed aubergines and methi muthia. Traditionally, the ingredients are layered in a clay pot and slow-cooked.
steps: Grind green garlic, coriander, coconut, sesame, spices and lemon into a coarse masala.
Stuff the aubergines and cut the other vegetables.
Make methi muthia with fenugreek leaves, gram flour and spices.
Layer vegetables and muthia in a heavy pot with masala and a little water.
Cover and cook slowly until tender; turn gently.
dishes.history: Undhiyu is closely tied to the winter harvest of south Gujarat, especially the food culture of Surat. When seasonal vegetables and fresh beans were plentiful, households brought them together for a generous shared meal. It became a special part of winter gatherings and Uttarayan celebrations, with families and neighbourhoods preparing the dish for guests and festivals.

dishes.name: Dhokla
dishes.descriptor: A soft, savoury steamed batter preparation
dishes.overview: Dhokla is a savoury steamed cake made from fermented rice-and-pulse batter or, in popular versions, gram flour. It is cut into pieces and finished with a mustard-seed and curry-leaf tempering.
ingredients: Rice and chana dal, or gram flour depending on style
Natural fermentation or fruit salt for quick versions
steps: For a fermented version, soak rice and chana dal, grind and leave until aerated.
Season with salt, ginger and chilli. Add fruit salt only for a quick version.
Pour into a greased pan and steam until set.
Cool slightly and cut into squares.
Temper mustard seeds, curry leaves and chillies in oil; pour over the dhokla.
dishes.history: Gujarati cooks developed a wide family of steamed and fermented snacks using grains and pulses. Earlier Gujarati food writing includes references to preparations related to dhokla, while household methods continued to evolve across communities. Over time, dhokla became part of the region's everyday farsan culture, sold by snack shops and served at home, gatherings and celebrations.

foodCulture.text: Rotli, rice, dal or kadhi, vegetables and farsan are common parts of meals. Dhokla, thepla and seasonal dishes such as undhiyu are well known; food preferences differ across Kutch, Saurashtra, central and southern Gujarat.

maharashtra.name: Maharashtra
maharashtra.tagline: From Deccan grain kitchens to Mumbai street stalls, food reflects regional life and migration.

dishes.name: Vada Pav
dishes.descriptor: Spiced potato fritter served in a soft bread roll
dishes.overview: A spiced potato fritter is coated in gram-flour batter, deep-fried and served inside a pav roll. Garlic chutney, green chutney and fried chilli are common accompaniments.
ingredients: Mustard seeds, turmeric and curry leaves
Dry garlic chutney and green chutney
steps: Boil and mash potatoes. Mix with a tempering of mustard seeds, curry leaves, turmeric, chilli, ginger and garlic.
Shape the potato mixture into balls.
Make a thick gram-flour batter with salt and turmeric.
Dip the balls in batter and deep-fry until crisp.
Serve inside pav with chutneys and fried chilli.
dishes.history: Vada pav became part of Mumbai's working-city food culture as railway commuters, mill workers and street vendors shaped a demand for inexpensive, filling food that could be eaten quickly. The meeting of a spiced potato vada with bakery pav suited the pace of the city. Dadar's Ashok Vaidya became one of the best-known names associated with its rise, and stalls across Mumbai carried it into everyday life.

regionalGeography.text: Maharashtra includes the Konkan coast, Western Ghats and the drier Deccan plateau. Heavy coastal monsoon rain supports rice and coconut, while black soils and irrigation inland support crops such as jowar, cotton, pulses and sugarcane.

foodCulture.text: Jowar or bajra bhakri, rice, varan-bhaat, pithla and seasonal vegetables are common. Coastal meals often include fish and coconut, while snacks such as vada pav and regional dishes vary across Konkan, Vidarbha, Marathwada and western Maharashtra.

karnataka.name: Karnataka
karnataka.tagline: A varied food culture, from coastal rice dishes to the millet traditions of the Deccan.

dishes.name: Mysore Pak
dishes.descriptor: A ghee-rich sweet of gram flour and sugar
dishes.overview: Mysore Pak is made by cooking gram flour with ghee and sugar syrup until it sets. It may be soft and porous or firmer and crumbly.

Prepare a sugar syrup.
Add the flour gradually, stirring to prevent lumps.
Add hot ghee in batches and stir until the mixture thickens.
Pour into a greased tray, set and cut while slightly warm.
dishes.history: Mysore Pak is remembered through the culinary traditions of the Mysore Palace during the Wadiyar era. Local accounts associate its creation with palace cook Kakasura Madappa, whose combination of gram flour, sugar and ghee became a favourite sweet. From palace kitchens the preparation entered Mysore's sweet shops, where confectioners developed the soft and firm styles enjoyed today.

dishes.history: Bisi bele bath belongs to the rice-and-lentil cooking tradition of the Mysuru region. Household cooks brought grains, pulses, vegetables and a roasted spice mixture together in a single nourishing meal, suited to family kitchens and communal dining. As Karnataka's tiffin houses and restaurants grew, the dish travelled well beyond its home region and became a familiar part of the state's food identity.

regionalGeography.text: Karnataka ranges from the wet Western Ghats and coast to the drier Deccan plateau. Red and laterite soils, black soils and river valleys support different crops, including rice, ragi, jowar, arecanut, coffee and spices.

foodCulture.text: Rice, ragi mudde, jowar rotti, dosa and idli are everyday staples in different areas. Bisi bele bath, Udupi vegetarian food and coastal seafood are well known; food habits vary between the coast, Malnad, northern and southern districts.

uttar-pradesh.name: Uttar Pradesh
uttar-pradesh.tagline: A broad food landscape shaped by the Ganga plains, pilgrimage towns and Awadh's kitchens.

dishes.name: Galouti Kebab
dishes.descriptor: Fine-textured minced meat kebab from Lucknow
dishes.overview: Finely minced meat is mixed with raw papaya, aromatics and spices, shaped into small patties and shallow-fried in ghee. It is often served with paratha or roomali roti.
steps: Grind the meat until very fine.
Mix with papaya, ginger-garlic, fried onion and spices.
Rest briefly so the papaya can tenderise the meat.
Shape into small, flat patties.
Cook gently in ghee until set and lightly browned.
dishes.history: Galouti kebab emerged from the celebrated kebab culture of Awadh, where cooks in Lucknow's elite kitchens refined minced-meat preparations with aromatic spices and delicate textures. The city's specialist cooks developed a rich repertoire of kebabs for royal tables and formal hospitality. From these kitchens, galouti became one of Lucknow's best-known culinary signatures and later a mainstay of its restaurants.

dishes.name: Awadhi Dum Pukht Biryani
dishes.descriptor: Rice and meat slowly cooked in a sealed vessel
dishes.overview: Marinated meat and partly cooked rice are layered in a heavy vessel, sealed with dough and cooked slowly. The trapped steam finishes the rice and meat together.
steps: Marinate the meat with yoghurt, ginger-garlic, fried onion and spices.
Parboil the rice with whole spices; drain while still firm.
Layer meat and rice in a heavy handi with herbs and ghee.
Seal the lid with dough to keep steam inside.
Cook over low heat until the meat and rice are done; rest before opening.
dishes.history: Lucknow's dum pukht tradition reflects the meeting of Persianate and North Indian courtly food cultures. Awadhi cooks adapted rice-and-meat preparations to local tastes, using sealed vessels and slow cooking to build aroma and tenderness. The method became closely associated with Nawabi hospitality and spread through the city's professional cooks, kitchens and restaurants.

foodCulture.text: Wheat rotis and rice are common staples, usually served with dal and vegetables. Awadhi kebabs and biryani, Braj sweets, eastern snacks and Bundelkhand dishes add regional variety to everyday home cooking.

assam.name: Assam
assam.tagline: A riverine cuisine of rice, freshwater fish, sour broths and banana-ash preparations.

dishes.name: Assamese Khar
dishes.descriptor: An alkaline preparation made with plant-ash filtrate
dishes.overview: Khar is both an alkaline cooking ingredient and dishes made with it. Kola khar is filtered from banana-plant ash and used in preparations with papaya, pulses or vegetables.

Cook papaya, pulses or vegetables until nearly tender.
Add a measured amount of khar filtrate and simmer briefly.
Serve with rice. Ingredients and methods vary by household.
dishes.history: Khar reflects a distinctive Assamese cooking tradition built around the knowledge of plant ash and alkaline extracts. Families learned to prepare kola khar from parts of the banana plant and use it to shape the flavour of everyday meals. The technique became a recognisable part of Assamese food culture, linking household knowledge of local plants with a regional style of cooking.

dishes.name: Masor Tenga
dishes.descriptor: Light, sour fish curry with seasonal ingredients
dishes.overview: A light fish curry with a gentle sourness. Tomato, lemon, thekera, elephant apple, roselle or raw mango may be used, depending on season and household.

Lightly fry the pieces in mustard oil; set aside.
Temper whole spices and add tomato or another souring ingredient.
Add water and simmer to make a light broth.
Return the fish and simmer gently until cooked; finish with chilli and herbs.
dishes.history: Assam's rivers and wetlands have made freshwater fish central to daily food culture. Cooks developed light sour preparations that suited the local catch and balanced the richness of fish with ingredients gathered or grown in different seasons. The use of tomato, thekera, elephant apple and other souring fruits gives each household and region its own version of masor tenga.

regionalGeography.text: The Brahmaputra and Barak valleys have fertile river soils, heavy monsoon rain and a humid climate. These conditions support rice fields, ponds and river fishing, while the hills and forests provide bamboo shoots, greens and seasonal produce.

foodCulture.text: Rice is the main staple, often eaten with fish, leafy vegetables and simple dals. Khar and masor tenga are well-known preparations; pork, fermented foods and bamboo shoots feature in some community traditions, which vary across Assam.

andhra-pradesh.name: Andhra Pradesh
andhra-pradesh.tagline: Coastal and river-valley food shaped by rice, chillies and tamarind.

dishes.name: Gongura Pachadi
dishes.descriptor: A sour chutney made from gongura leaves
dishes.overview: Gongura pachadi is made from sour sorrel leaves cooked with chillies and garlic, then ground into a coarse chutney. It is commonly eaten with rice and ghee and is especially associated with the Guntur region.
steps: Wash the leaves and dry them well.
Cook the leaves in a little oil until soft.
Fry the chillies and garlic; add optional spices.
Grind or pound everything with salt into a coarse chutney.
Serve with rice and ghee.
dishes.history: Gongura became one of the defining flavours of Andhra kitchens, particularly in the Guntur region where the sour leaves are widely used. Household cooks turned the seasonal greens into chutneys and pickles that could be kept and enjoyed with rice through the year. The preparation's strong flavour and everyday presence helped make gongura a marker of Andhra food identity.

dishes.name: Pootharekulu
dishes.descriptor: A paper-thin rice sweet from Atreyapuram
dishes.overview: Pootharekulu is made by wrapping sugar or jaggery, ghee and sometimes nuts in very thin rice sheets. It is closely associated with Atreyapuram in the Godavari delta and is also known as Andhra's paper sweet.

Spread a very thin layer over a heated surface and lift the dried sheet carefully.
Add sugar or jaggery and ghee, with optional nuts.
Fold the sheet into a small parcel and allow it to cool.
dishes.history: Pootharekulu grew into a celebrated sweet of Atreyapuram in the Godavari delta, where rice-growing households developed a highly skilled way of making delicate rice sheets. The work of preparing and folding the thin layers became a craft passed through families and local sweet makers. The village's reputation for the paper-like sweet spread across Andhra Pradesh, and its GI recognition strengthened its regional identity.

foodCulture.text: Rice meals with pappu, pulusu, pachadi and pickles are common. Coastal food often includes fish and seafood, while Rayalaseema is known for spicier dishes and greater use of millets and groundnuts.

Mix in the prepared starter culture.
Keep the mixture in a clean container to ferment.
After fermentation, strain or press the mixture to collect the drink.
dishes.history: Rice fermentation is part of the household knowledge of several communities in Arunachal Pradesh. Families prepare apong for social visits, community gatherings, festivals and important ceremonies, using starter cultures whose preparation is passed between generations. The drink reflects the place of rice in local agriculture and the way food and hospitality are woven into community life.

dishes.descriptor: Roasted wheat balls with mashed vegetables
dishes.overview: Litti are wheat balls filled with roasted gram flour (sattu), spices and mustard oil. They are roasted over heat and served with chokha, a mash of roasted brinjal, potato or tomato seasoned with garlic, chillies and mustard oil.
steps: Knead wheat flour with water into a firm dough.
Mix sattu with mustard oil, garlic, chillies and salt.
Fill dough portions with the sattu mixture and shape into balls.
Roast until cooked through and browned.
Roast the vegetables, mash with seasoning and serve as chokha.
dishes.history: Litti chokha is rooted in the agrarian foodways of the Bhojpuri region, where wheat, roasted gram and seasonal vegetables shaped everyday meals. The sattu-filled litti could be roasted over a household fire and carried easily by farmers and travellers. It later moved from village kitchens into town markets and street stalls, becoming one of Bihar's best-known foods.

Roll it into thin sheets and layer or fold them.
Cut into pieces and deep-fry until crisp.
Coat or soak the pieces in sugar syrup and allow to cool.

Local confectioners built a reputation for its delicate layers and crisp texture, passing the careful preparation from one generation of sweet makers to the next. The sweet remains a recognised specialty of the area.

chhattisgarh.name: Chhattisgarh

Grind with water into a smooth batter.
Add salt and optional herbs or chilli.
Spread on a hot, lightly oiled griddle and cook both sides.
Serve with chutney or curd.
dishes.history: Chila reflects the importance of rice and lentils in Chhattisgarh's household food traditions. Cooks turned familiar grains into a simple griddle meal that could be prepared in village kitchens and served as breakfast or a light snack. Its place in everyday cooking helped it move from home meals into local stalls and community food gatherings.

goa.name: Goa
goa.tagline: A Konkan coastal cuisine shaped by seafood, coconut and Portuguese-era exchange.

dishes.name: Xacuti
dishes.descriptor: A Goan curry made with roasted spices and coconut
dishes.overview: Xacuti is a rich curry made with roasted spices, coconut and onion. It may be prepared with chicken, meat, seafood or vegetables. It is commonly served with rice or local breads.

Grind with garlic, ginger and turmeric into a paste.
Cook the onion until soft, then add the main ingredient.
Add the paste and water; simmer until cooked and thickened.
Serve with rice or Goan bread.

Household cooks developed richly roasted masalas for family meals and celebrations, with variations across communities. The curry became one of the recognisable preparations of Goan home and restaurant cooking.

haryana.tagline: A wheat-and-millet cuisine shaped by dry plains and dairy farming.

Finish with ghee and serve with butter, jaggery or buttermilk.

Bajra khichdi became closely associated with the season, village life and harvest celebrations, including Makar Sankranti.

Leave it to ferment and rise.

Steam until cooked; serve hot with ghee or curry.
dishes.history: Siddu belongs to the wheat-growing food traditions of Himachal's hill communities. Families adapted familiar bread-making skills to the mountain climate, using fermentation and steaming to prepare a substantial meal for cold days. Fillings and accompaniments vary between households, and the bread moved from village kitchens into local eateries as a familiar expression of Pahari cooking.

dishes.descriptor: A deep-fried rice-and-lentil pancake
dishes.overview: Dhuska is a crisp, deep-fried snack made from soaked rice and lentils. It is commonly served with potato curry, gram curry or chutney and is popular in Jharkhand.
steps: Soak rice and lentils, then grind with water into a thick batter.
Mix in salt and optional aromatics.
Fry small portions until golden and crisp.
Serve hot with curry or chutney.
dishes.history: Dhuska grew from the rice-and-pulse food culture of Jharkhand, where household cooks turned everyday grains into a crisp snack for family meals and gatherings. Its popularity spread through local markets and town food stalls, where it is often served with curry. The snack remains a familiar part of the region's street-food identity.

dishes.descriptor: A wild mushroom preparation from the monsoon forests
dishes.overview: Rugra, also called rugda, is a wild mushroom gathered during the monsoon, especially near sal forests. It is cooked as a spiced curry and valued as a seasonal food by local communities.

Simmer until tender and serve with rice.
dishes.history: Rugra is tied to the monsoon cycle of Jharkhand's sal forests. Adivasi and other local communities gather the seasonal mushrooms as part of a wider knowledge of edible forest foods, then bring them to village markets and household kitchens. Its short season gives rugra a special place in local food culture and connects the harvest to the rhythms of the forest.

dishes.name: Indori Poha
dishes.descriptor: A flattened-rice breakfast associated with Indore
dishes.overview: Indori poha is flattened rice cooked with onion, potato, peanuts, spices and lemon. It is a signature Indore breakfast, often served with sev and jalebi.
steps: Rinse and drain the flattened rice.
Temper mustard seeds and curry leaves; cook onion and potato until soft.
Add turmeric, salt and poha; toss until heated through.
Finish with lemon and peanuts; serve with sev or jalebi.
dishes.history: Flattened rice has long been eaten across central India, but Indore's markets and street vendors gave poha a distinctive local identity. Vendors built a recognisable breakfast ritual around sev, jeeravan, onions and lemon, often paired with jalebi. The combination became part of the city's morning food culture and a point of pride for Indore.

dishes.descriptor: A Malwa wheat-and-lentil meal of boiled, baked dough balls
dishes.overview: Dal bafla is a Malwa meal of wheat-flour balls that are boiled, then baked or roasted. They are served with lentils, ghee and chutney; the boiling step gives bafla a softer centre than baati.
steps: Knead flour, ghee, salt and water into a firm dough.
Shape into balls and boil until partly cooked.
Roast or bake until the outside is crisp.
Cook the dal with spices and serve with bafla, ghee and chutney.
dishes.history: Dal bafla is a Malwa expression of the wider wheat-and-lentil food culture shared across central and western India. Local cooks adapted the idea of baati to Malwa kitchens, using a preparation that produces a softer centre and serving it with dal and ghee. The meal became a familiar part of family feasts and regional restaurant menus.

dishes.descriptor: A Meitei mashed vegetable and fermented-fish dish
dishes.overview: Eromba, or iromba, is a Meitei dish of boiled vegetables mashed with chillies and fermented fish called ngari. It is usually eaten with rice and has a strong, savoury flavour.
steps: Boil or steam the vegetables until soft.
Roast or soften the chillies.
Mash the vegetables with chillies and salt.
Mix in ngari and serve with rice.
dishes.history: Eromba reflects the central place of ngari in Meitei food culture. Fermented fish developed as a valued way to preserve the catch and bring a deep savoury flavour to household meals. Cooks combined it with vegetables and chillies from the kitchen garden, creating a dish that became a familiar accompaniment to rice and a marker of Manipuri cooking.

dishes.descriptor: A black-rice pudding from Manipur
dishes.overview: Chak hao kheer is a pudding made with Manipur’s aromatic black rice, milk and sugar. Its deep purple colour comes from pigments in the rice, and it is served at feasts and family ceremonies.

Cook it in water until tender.
Add milk and sugar; simmer until thick.
Finish with cardamom and optional nuts or raisins.
dishes.history: Chak hao is an aromatic black rice cultivated in Manipur and valued in both everyday and ceremonial food traditions. Its striking colour and fragrance made it a special grain for family celebrations, community feasts and festive offerings. Preparing it as kheer brought the local rice into a celebratory sweet, while growers and cooks continue to preserve its place in Manipuri food culture.

dishes.descriptor: Khasi rice cooked with meat and spices
dishes.overview: Jadoh is rice cooked with pork or chicken, turmeric, ginger and aromatic leaves. It is eaten in Khasi homes and at community gatherings, often with chutney or pickle.
steps: Cook the meat with ginger, onion, turmeric and bay leaf.
Add washed rice and enough water.
Simmer until the rice is tender and absorbs the meat's flavour.
Serve hot with chutney or pickle.
dishes.history: Jadoh is closely connected to Khasi food culture, where rice and pork have long been part of home meals and communal gatherings. The one-pot preparation reflects the practical cooking of hill households and the importance of shared food at community occasions. It also became a familiar part of Shillong's market and restaurant culture, carrying Khasi flavours to new audiences.

dishes.overview: Tungrymbai is made from cooked soybeans fermented in leaf-lined baskets, often near a fireplace. The beans are then cooked with onion, ginger, garlic and chillies, and served with rice.

Pack them in a leaf-lined basket and ferment for several days.
Cook the fermented beans with onion, ginger, garlic and chillies.
Serve with rice.

Boil them with salt and water until tender.
Add fermented pork fat or optional seasonings.
Simmer briefly and serve with rice.
dishes.history: Bai grew out of Mizo household cooking, where meals draw on seasonal greens, garden vegetables and ingredients gathered from the surrounding hills. Its place at the family table reflects a tradition of simple, shared cooking built around local produce.

dishes.overview: Pork is smoked over a hearth and cooked with bamboo shoots, chillies and local herbs. The dish is commonly served with rice and reflects Naga traditions of smoking and preserving food.

Clean and slice the bamboo shoots.
Cook the pork with bamboo shoots, chillies and salt.
Simmer until tender and serve with rice.
dishes.history: Smoking meat over the hearth is a long-standing food practice across Naga communities, allowing households to preserve pork between occasions when fresh meat was available. Bamboo shoots, gathered seasonally from nearby forests, became a natural partner in stews and shared meals. The combination reflects the close relationship between Naga cooking, forest produce and communal food traditions.

Over generations, household and temple food traditions helped make dalma one of Odisha's best-known preparations.

Pack them in a bamboo container or earthen pot.
Allow them to ferment.
Use the fermented fish in curries, chutneys or vegetable dishes.
Serve the cooked preparation with rice.
dishes.history: Mui borok reflects the importance of fermented fish in Tripuri food traditions. Preserving fish allowed households to keep the flavour of the catch and use it to season meals beyond the fishing season. The preparation became a defining part of Indigenous Tripuri cooking, appearing in household curries, chutneys and shared meals with rice.

dishes.name: Chakhwi
dishes.descriptor: A bamboo-shoot and meat preparation of Tripura
dishes.overview: Chakhwi is a Tripuri dish made with bamboo shoots, local herbs and sometimes meat or fish. It is lightly cooked, usually with little oil, and served with rice.

Cook with meat or fish, chillies and aromatics.
Simmer until tender and serve with rice.
dishes.history: Chakhwi reflects Tripura's Indigenous use of bamboo shoots and seasonal ingredients gathered from the surrounding landscape. Families developed variations using local herbs and, in some homes, meat or fish. The dish remains part of everyday Tripuri food culture and shows how forest produce and household knowledge shape regional cooking.

regionalGeography.text: Tripura’s hill ranges and river valleys have warm, humid monsoon conditions. Rice is grown in the valleys, while bamboo, fruit and vegetables grow in hill areas; rivers and ponds provide fish for local meals.

foodCulture.text: Rice is the staple, commonly eaten with fish, vegetables and fermented berma. Mui borok, chakhwi and bamboo-shoot preparations are familiar in Indigenous Tripuri food traditions, alongside Bengali food traditions in the state.

uttarakhand.name: Uttarakhand
uttarakhand.tagline: A Kumaoni and Garhwali food culture of millets, lentils and mountain greens.

dishes.name: Kafuli
dishes.descriptor: A thick green spinach-and-fenugreek preparation from Uttarakhand
dishes.overview: Kafuli is a thick green preparation made with spinach, fenugreek and other leafy greens. Garlic, chillies and rice flour add flavour and body; it is served with rice or roti.
steps: Wash and chop the greens.
Boil or steam until soft, then mash or grind.
Cook with garlic, chillies and salt.
Stir in rice flour and simmer until thick.
Serve with rice or roti.
dishes.history: Kafuli grew from the food traditions of Kumaon and Garhwal, where terraced farms and kitchen gardens supplied leafy greens for much of the year. Household cooks turned seasonal greens into a substantial meal using familiar grains and local dairy. The dish became a valued part of hill cooking, especially when families gathered around the winter hearth.

dishes.name: Bal Mithai
dishes.descriptor: A Kumaoni sweet of roasted khoya coated in sugar balls
dishes.overview: Bal mithai is a Kumaoni sweet made from slowly roasted khoya and coated in small white sugar balls. It is especially associated with Almora.

Mix in sugar and optional cardamom.
Shape into a block and allow it to cool slightly.
Coat with small sugar balls.
Cut into pieces and serve.
dishes.history: Bal mithai became a signature sweet of Almora through the work of local halwais and the town's traditional sweet shops. Its roasted khoya centre and sugar-coated finish made it distinctive among Kumaoni sweets. As visitors and traders carried it beyond the hill town, bal mithai became one of the best-known edible symbols of Almora.

regionalGeography.text: Uttarakhand ranges from high Himalayan slopes to the warmer Terai plains. Terraced mountain farms grow millets, pulses and seasonal vegetables, while deeper lowland soils support more rice and wheat; winters are cold at higher elevations.

foodCulture.text: Mandua, jhangora, rice and wheat are eaten in different areas, often with lentils and local greens. Kafuli, chainsoo and phanu are familiar dishes, with Kumaoni, Garhwali and Terai food traditions differing.

andaman-and-nicobar-islands.name: Andaman and Nicobar Islands
andaman-and-nicobar-islands.tagline: Island foodways shaped by seafood, coconut, tubers and migration.

dishes.name: Andaman Fish Curry
dishes.descriptor: A coastal fish curry served with rice
dishes.overview: A flexible island-style curry made with locally caught fish, coconut, chilli and souring ingredients. Recipes vary across communities and islands, reflecting the region's seafood economy and the influence of Bengali and South Indian cooking. It is commonly served with rice.
steps: Clean and portion the fish.
Prepare a curry base with chilli, turmeric, tamarind and aromatics.
Add coconut milk or coconut and enough water to form a light gravy.
Add the fish and simmer gently until cooked.
Adjust seasoning and serve with rice.
dishes.history: The Andaman Islands' food culture has been shaped by the sea and by communities who arrived from different parts of the Indian mainland. Bengali, Tamil and other regional cooking traditions met the island's fresh catch and local produce, creating many styles of fish curry. The dish is best understood as part of this layered coastal food culture, rather than one fixed island recipe.

dishes.overview: Nicobari aloo refers to traditional yam varieties cultivated and prepared by Nicobarese communities. Tubers are important carbohydrate foods alongside coconut, pig and marine foods. Cut it into manageable pieces.
Boil or roast until tender, following local household practice.
Serve with coconut or other locally prepared foods.
dishes.history: Tubers have an important place in Nicobarese food systems, alongside coconut, fishing and animal husbandry. Families cultivate and prepare local varieties as part of everyday meals and village celebrations, passing knowledge of the crops through generations. Nicobari aloo reflects the close relationship between island agriculture, community life and the foods grown in local gardens.

foodCulture.text: Rice, fish, seafood, coconut and tubers are common foods, though traditions differ between the island groups. Nicobari foodways include distinctive local ingredients and practices, while migrant communities have brought other regional cuisines.

chandigarh.name: Chandigarh
chandigarh.tagline: A planned city with Punjabi, Haryanvi and contemporary urban food influences.

dishes.name: Chole Bhature
dishes.descriptor: Spiced chickpeas with deep-fried leavened bread
dishes.overview: Chole bhature pairs chickpeas simmered in a spiced gravy with puffy, deep-fried bread. It is a popular breakfast and street-food choice in Chandigarh, reflecting the city's Punjabi food culture rather than a dish invented locally.
steps: Soak and cook the chickpeas until tender.
Prepare a masala with onion, tomato, ginger, garlic and spices.
Simmer the chickpeas in the masala.
Make and rest a soft dough for the bhature.
Roll and deep-fry the breads until puffed; serve hot with chole.
dishes.history: Chandigarh's food culture grew with the people who settled in the planned city, including families carrying Punjabi cooking traditions from across the region. Dhabas, markets and neighbourhood eateries made chole bhature a familiar meal for residents and visitors. The dish became part of the city's everyday Punjabi dining scene while retaining its wider North Indian roots.

dishes.name: Amritsari Kulcha
dishes.descriptor: A stuffed Punjabi flatbread baked in a tandoor
dishes.overview: Amritsari kulcha is a leavened flatbread stuffed with potato, onion or paneer and baked in a tandoor. Served with chole, chutney or butter, it is associated with Amritsar but is widely enjoyed in Chandigarh's Punjabi-influenced food scene.
steps: Prepare a soft dough and let it rest.

Fill and roll the dough into a flatbread.

Brush with ghee or butter and serve with chole.
dishes.history: Amritsari kulcha travelled beyond its home city through Punjabi migration, trade and the growth of tandoor bakeries and restaurants. In Chandigarh, cooks and food businesses carried the stuffed bread into neighbourhood eateries, where it became a popular partner for chole. Its presence reflects the shared food culture linking Chandigarh with Amritsar and the wider Punjab region.

regionalGeography.text: Chandigarh lies on the northern plains near the Shivalik foothills, but urban growth leaves little farmland within the city. Its food supply is closely linked to the surrounding irrigated Punjab and Haryana plains.

foodCulture.text: Wheat breads, rice, dal, dairy foods and North Indian vegetables are common. Punjabi and Haryanvi dishes, tandoori foods, chickpea snacks and street food are widely available, reflecting the city’s mixed urban population.

classification.definition: An edible fruit consumed fresh. It is catalogued here as a regional food-heritage record, not as a prepared dish or recipe.

dishes.overview: Hoka fruit is the ripe edible fruit of the branching Hoka palm associated with Diu. The Diu–Daman tourism brochure describes the ripe fruit as deep red, sweet-and-sour and firm, with hard, fibrous flesh. It says the fruit is popular among local residents and can be obtained from local vendors. This entry records the fruit as a local food resource rather than presenting it as a cooked dish.
dishes.foodCharacteristics: The local tourism brochure describes the ripe fruit as deep red, with a sweet-and-sour taste and hard, fibrous flesh. These are the characteristics reported by that source; the archive does not infer a specific variety or botanical measurement.
dishes.consumption: The brochure recommends tasting the ripe fruit and reports that local vendors sell it. It does not provide a recipe or a detailed preparation method, so this record does not invent one.
dishes.history: The Hoka palm became part of Diu's landscape through the maritime connections of the Portuguese period, when traders brought the tree from the African region. Over time it adapted to the island environment and its fruit entered local food life, sold by vendors and enjoyed by residents. The palm now forms a distinctive part of Diu's coastal identity.

Fold or roll the bread around the filling and serve warm.

Accounts connect the preparation with a Bengali cook who brought the idea of a kathi-style roll and used fillings suited to Daman, including seafood. Local vendors carried the variation into the town's casual food scene around markets and the jetty.

delhi.name: Delhi

dishes.name: Butter Chicken

dishes.overview: Butter chicken, or murgh makhani, combines tandoor-cooked chicken with a smooth tomato-and-butter sauce. It is closely associated with Moti Mahal in Daryaganj and Delhi's post-Partition restaurant culture. Its creamy gravy and smoky chicken made it a widely copied restaurant dish.

Roast or grill the chicken until cooked and lightly charred.
Cook tomatoes with butter and spices to make the gravy.
Blend or strain the gravy, then add the chicken.
Simmer briefly and finish with cream if desired.
dishes.history: Butter chicken is closely associated with the Punjabi restaurant culture that took root in post-Partition Delhi. At Moti Mahal in Daryaganj, cooks built on the city's tandoor tradition by serving cooked chicken in a rich tomato-and-butter gravy. The dish travelled through restaurant kitchens across India and became one of Delhi's most recognised contributions to popular dining.

Chandni Chowk's food lanes brought together fried snacks, pulses, potatoes, yoghurt and chutneys in countless combinations. Generations of street sellers developed local specialties, making chaat part of the everyday rhythm of the old city.

foodCulture.text: Wheat breads, rice, dal and vegetables are everyday foods. Old Delhi is known for chaat, kebabs, biryani and sweets, while Punjabi, Mughlai and many migrant cuisines contribute to the city’s varied food culture.

jammu-and-kashmir.tagline: A Himalayan food culture with Kashmiri Pandit, Muslim and Wazwan traditions.

dishes.name: Rogan Josh

dishes.overview: Rogan josh is a slow-cooked lamb curry flavoured with Kashmiri chillies, fennel, ginger and other spices. Recipes differ between Kashmiri Pandit and Muslim traditions, including their use of garlic, yogurt and colouring agents. It is also recognised as a Wazwan dish.

Add whole spices, ginger and ground Kashmiri chilli.
Add water or yogurt according to the chosen regional style.
Simmer slowly until the lamb is tender and the gravy is aromatic.
Serve with rice.
dishes.history: Rogan josh reflects the layers of influence that shaped Kashmiri cooking, including Persian and Central Asian culinary connections adapted to local ingredients. Kashmiri cooks made the lamb preparation part of the elaborate Wazwan tradition, where dishes are served as a carefully arranged communal feast. Distinct Pandit and Muslim styles continue to give the dish regional depth.

dishes.overview: Skyu is a hearty Ladakhi stew made with small pieces of wheat dough simmered with root vegetables. Meat may be added, while vegetarian versions are also prepared. Its thick, warming consistency suits the cold climate and makes it a distinctive local comfort food.

dishes.history: Skyu grew within the food traditions of Ladakhi farming communities, where barley and wheat, root vegetables and stored produce shaped meals through the cold season. foodCulture.text: Barley, wheat, buckwheat and local vegetables are important foods. Skyu, khambir bread, thukpa, momos and butter tea are familiar, while food habits vary between villages and Buddhist and Muslim communities.

Season with chilli, coriander, cardamom and salt.

Add the tuna and cook until done, allowing the spices to coat it.
Serve with rice or flatbread.
dishes.history: Mus kavaab reflects Minicoy's close maritime and cultural connections with the Maldives. Fishing, especially tuna fishing, has long shaped the island's work and food traditions, while shared seafaring links brought related tastes and cooking ideas across the sea. The preparation became a distinctive part of Minicoy's household cuisine and island hospitality.

dishes.overview: Maas podichathu combines dried tuna with coconut, turmeric, onion and garlic. It draws on Lakshadweep's tuna fishery and the preservation of fish for later use. The preparation is a flavourful accompaniment to rice and other island dishes.

dishes.name: Roll Roti
dishes.descriptor: A local bakery bread linked to Franco-Tamil household foodways
dishes.overview: Roll roti is a bread associated with older wood-fired bakeries in Puducherry. Tamil cooks supplied bread to French and Creole households, and it was eaten with sweetened tea or coconut milk. The preparation is a record of everyday exchange rather than simply a French dish transplanted to India.
ingredients: Coconut milk or tea to serve
steps: Mix flour, water, salt and leavening into a dough.
Knead and rest until the dough becomes workable.
Shape into small rolls or flat rounds.
Bake in a hot oven until cooked and lightly browned.
Serve with tea or coconut milk, as preferred.
dishes.history: Roll roti reflects the everyday food exchange of colonial Puducherry, where Tamil bakers supplied bread to French and Creole households and to local workers. Wood-fired bakeries became part of the town's neighbourhood life, blending local baking skills with changing tastes. The bread remains a reminder of how Tamil cooks shaped the food culture of the former French settlement.

dishes.name: Vettu Sambar
dishes.descriptor: A simple Tamil home-style sambar from Puducherry foodways
dishes.overview: Vettu sambar is a quick, economical home-style preparation described in accounts of Puducherry's Tamil food culture. It is flavoured with chilli and common pantry ingredients and served with hot rice. Family methods vary, reflecting its place in everyday cooking rather than restaurant cuisine.
steps: Cook the toor dal until soft.
Prepare tamarind water and add chilli and turmeric.
Simmer the tamarind mixture with onion and optional tomato.
Add the cooked dal and simmer until combined.
Temper with mustard seeds and serve with rice.
dishes.history: Vettu sambar belongs to the everyday Tamil food traditions of Puducherry, where household cooks made filling meals from familiar pantry ingredients. Its place in family kitchens reflects a style of practical home cooking that continued alongside the bakery and restaurant cultures shaped by the town's colonial history. The preparation survives through household variation and shared local memory.

regionalGeography.text: Puducherry’s four separated enclaves have different coastal and river settings. The Cauvery delta supports rice, while the coast provides fish and coconut; hot weather, monsoon rain and local waterlogging shape farming and fishing seasons.

foodCulture.text: Rice meals, sambar, seafood and local vegetables are common in Puducherry and Karaikal. Mahe shares Kerala food influences, Yanam reflects Telugu traditions, and Puducherry’s bakeries preserve elements of Franco-Tamil food culture.
